{{Short description|Numerals used in the eastern Arab world and Asia}}
{{For|Western Arabic Numerals|Arabic numerals}}
{{Numeral systems}}
[[File:The_Brahmi_numeral_system_and_its_descendants.png|alt=|thumb|Evolution of Indian numerals into Arabic and Eastern Arabic numerals along with their adoption in [[Europe]]]]
The '''Eastern Arabic numerals''', also called '''Indo-Arabic numerals''', or '''Arabic–Indic numerals''', as designated by [[Unicode]], are the symbols used to represent [[numerical digits]] in conjunction with the [[Arabic script]] in the countries of the [[Mashriq]] (the east of the [[Arab world]], including the [[Arabian Peninsula]]), and the variants in other countries that use the [[Persian numerals]] in [[greater Iran]] and [[Asia]].

The early [[Hindu–Arabic numeral system]] used a variety of shapes.<ref>{{cite book |first=Paul |last= Kunitzsch |chapter=The Transmission of Hindu–Arabic Numerals Reconsidered |editor1=J. P. Hogendijk |editor2=A. I. Sabra |title=The Enterprise of Science in Islam: New Perspectives |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_AUtLNtg3nsC&pg=PA3 |year=2003 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-19482-2 |pages=3–22}}</ref> It is unknown when the Western Arabic numeral shapes diverged from those of Eastern Arabic numerals. The Western digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 9 are clearly related, but the origins of 6, 7 and 8 are obscure.<ref>{{cite book |first=Paul |last= Kunitzsch |chapter=The Transmission of Hindu–Arabic Numerals Reconsidered |editor1=J. P. Hogendijk |editor2=A. I. Sabra |title=The Enterprise of Science in Islam: New Perspectives |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_AUtLNtg3nsC&pg=PA3 |year=2003 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-19482-2 |pages=3–22}}</ref>

== Origin ==
The numeral system originates from an ancient [[Indian numerals|Indian numeral system]], which was reintroduced{{to whom?|date=August 2025}}{{when|date=August 2025}} during the [[Islamic Golden Age]] in the book ''On the Calculation with Hindic Numerals'' written by the [[Persians|Persian]] mathematician and engineer [[Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi|al-Khwarizmi]], whose name was [[Latinisation of names|Latinized]] as ''Algoritmi''.<ref group="note">Other Latin transliterations include ''Algaurizin''.{{citation needed|date=August 2015}}</ref>

== Other names ==
These numbers are known as {{lang|ar-Latn|ʾarqām mašriqiyya}} ({{lang|ar|أَرْقَام مَشْرِقِيَّة}}) or {{lang|ar-Latn|ʾarqām hindiyya}} ({{lang|ar|أَرْقَام هِنْدِيَّة}}) in [[Arabic]]. They are sometimes also called Indic numerals<ref>{{cite web |title=Glossary of Unicode terms |website=[[IBM]] |url=https://www.ibm.com/developerworks/library/glossaries/unicode.html#indic_numerals |access-date=2 September 2015}}</ref> or Arabic–Indic numerals<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arabic–Indic Numerals / أرقام هندية - Learn Arabic with Polly Lingual |url=https://pollylingu.al/ar/en/lessons/2150 |access-date=2023-03-15 |website=pollylingu.al |language=en}}</ref> in English. However, that is sometimes discouraged as it can lead to confusion with [[Indian numerals|Devanagari numerals]], used in [[Brahmic scripts]] of the [[Indian subcontinent]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.unicode.org/glossary/|title=Glossary|access-date=2 September 2015}}</ref>

== Numerals ==
{{See also|Modern Arabic mathematical notation}}[[File:clock-in-cairo-with-eastern-arabic-numerals.jpg|thumb|Eastern Arabic numerals on a clock in the [[Cairo Metro]]]]Each numeral in the Persian variant has a different [[Unicode]] point even if it looks identical to the Eastern Arabic numeral counterpart.<ref>{{Cite web |last=About numbers in Iran |date=2021-01-25 |title=Persian numbers |url=https://en.tourinpersia.com/learn-persian-language/persian-numbers/ |website=en-US}}</ref> However, the variants used with [[Urdu]] and other [[languages of South Asia]] are not encoded separately from the Persian variants.

|}Written numerals are arranged with their lowest-value digit to the right, with higher value positions added to the left. That is identical to the arrangement used for [[Western Arabic numerals]], even though Arabic script is read from [[right-to-left]].<ref name="karl">{{cite book |last=Menninger |first=Karl |title=Number words and number symbols: a cultural history of numbers |year=1992 |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |isbn=0-486-27096-3 |pages=415 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YLJb6-OyUIQC&pg=PA415 }}</ref> Columns of numbers are usually arranged with the decimal points aligned.

In Arabic, negative signs are written to the right of magnitudes, e.g. {{lang|ar|−٣}} (−3). In Persian, they are written to the left, e.g. {{lang|ar|٣−}}.[[File:Peugeot_Pars_Face.jpg|thumb|Eastern Arabic letters and numerals on the [[Vehicle registration plates of Iran|license plate of a car in Iran]], which reads "82N712-11" |left]]In-line fractions are written with the numerator on the left and the denominator on the right of the fraction slash, e.g. {{lang|ar| ٢/٧ }} ({{frac|2|7}}).

The Arabic decimal separator {{char|٫}} (U+066B) or the comma {{char|,}} is used as the [[decimal mark]], as in {{lang|ar| ٣٫١٤١٥٩٢٦٥٣٥٨ }} ([[pi|3.14159265358]]).

The Arabic thousands separator {{char|٬}} (U+066C) or quote {{char|'}} or Arabic comma {{char|،}} (U+060C) may be used as a [[decimal mark#Digit grouping|thousands separator]], e.g. {{lang|ar| ١٬٠٠٠٬٠٠٠٬٠٠٠ }} (1,000,000,000).

== Contemporary use ==
{{Multiple image
| direction         = horizontal
| image1            = Urdu numeral four.svg
| image2            = Urdu numeral seven.svg
| total_width       = 180
| align             = right
| caption1          = Urdu numeral {{lang|ur|۴}} (4)
| caption2          = Urdu numeral {{lang|ur|۷}} (7)

Eastern Arabic numerals are predominantly used over Western Arabic numerals in many countries to the east of the [[Arab world]], notably [[Iran]] and [[Afghanistan]].

Both Eastern and Western Arabic numerals are concurrently used (and are often employed alongside each other) across Arabic-speaking Asia, [[Egypt]] and [[Sudan]], although Western Arabic numerals are increasingly favoured in the region, particularly in [[Saudi Arabia]]. The [[United Arab Emirates]] uses both Eastern and Western Arabic numerals.

In [[Pakistan]], Western Arabic numerals are more extensively used digitally. Eastern numerals continue to see use in [[Urdu]] publications and newspapers, as well as signboards.{{Clarify|reason=So, are the Eastern numerals used or not? Needs a clearer explanation, and if possible, a citation. |date=December 2020}}

In the [[Maghreb]], only Western Arabic numerals are commonly used today. In medieval times, this region used a slightly different variation of the system (from which, via [[Italy]], Western Arabic numerals derive).

The [[Thaana]] writing system used for the [[Dhivehi language|Maldivian language]] adopted its first nine letters (''haa'', ''shaviyani'', ''noonu'', ''raa'', ''baa'', ''ihaviyani'', ''kaafu'', ''alifu'', and ''vaavu'') from Perso-Arabic numerals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gippert |first=Jost |date=2013 |editor-last=Chen |editor-first=Shu-Fen |editor2-last=Slade |editor2-first=Benjamin |title=An Outline of the History of Maldivian Writing |url=http://saruna.mnu.edu.mv/jspui/bitstream/123456789/12120/1/An%20outline%20of%20the%20history%20of%20Maldivian%20writing.pdf |journal=Grammatica et Verba Glamor and Verve - Studies in South Asian, Historical, and Indo-Europea Linguistics in Honor O Hans Henrich Hock on the Occasion of His Seventy-fifth Birthday |publisher=Beech Stave Press |publication-place=Ann Arbor |pages=96–98 |isbn=978-0-9895142-0-0 |oclc=852488593 |via=[[Maldives National University]]}}</ref>
